newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FORECAST - REAL WAGES KEY TO HUNGARY GDP - THINK-TANK.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - REAL WAGES KEY TO HUNGARY GDP - THINK-TANK.

text.p: Disappointing growth figures for this year should lead Hungary to ease on its eighteen month old austerity programme, Kopint-Datorg Rt, one of the country's main economic think-tanks, said on Thursday.

Deputy chief executive Andras Koves said Hungary reduced inflation and its current account and budget deficits in the past two years and the gross domestic product (GDP) could grow by 0.5 to one percent in 1996 and two percent in 1997.
But to achieve this the government must stop a trend of decline in real wages and household consumption, keeping to its annual inflation forecast next year, he told a news conference.
"If this trend will continue for a long time, this may threaten the improvement of balances which have already been achieved," he said.

Kopint-Datorg said the government helped the business sector to become more profitable in 1995 and 1996, but it was disappointing that enterprises, discouraged by low domestic demand, did not spend their surplus revenues for investments.
"Among 1996 economic processes, perhaps investments show the most worrying picture," the think-tank said in a statement.
Kopint-Datorg forecasts investments to increase by three percent this year, while household consumption would decrease by two to three percent after a drop of six percent in 1995.

The think-tank said real wages were likely to drop by five to six percent in 1996 compared with the two percent government plan because inflation will drop from last year's 28.2 percent only to 23-24 percent in 1996 and not 20 percent as targeted.
Koves said the government should calculate inflation for 1997 more carefully to prevent a further drop in real wages.
However, Kopint-Datorg said inflation is likely to drop only to levels between 19 and 21 percent next year, compared with the 18 percent government target.
The think-tank expects Hungary's imports to increase six to seven percent next year, while exports should grow nine to 10 percent but this would fall short of making the GDP grow.

But if real wages preserve their real value in 1997 and communal consumption will be cut by only five to six percent instead of the planned 10 percent, investments could increase by five to six percent and the GDP would grow by two percent, Kopint-Datorg said.
